3. Funding for Working Capital Requirement 
 
With the growth in our business operations, our Company requires additional working capital, as the 
industry in which we operate is working capital intensive. Historically, we have funded a significant 
portion of our working capital requirements through a combination of bank borrowings and internal 
accruals. In order to support incremental business growth, we propose to utilize ₹3,400.00 lakhs from 
the Net Proceeds of the Issue to meet the incremental working capital requirements of our Company. 
 
Our Company is primarily engaged in the manufacturing and fabrication of re -rolled structural steel 
products including Angles, Channels, MS Sections, Flats & Rods and engineered steel products and trading 
of steel products. Our products cater to railway electrification and power & energy infrastructure as well 
as various other industries. 
 
With a view to strengthening its forward integration, the Company acquired the manufacturing unit of BSL 
Railtrack Engineers Private Limited which is now known as Manufacturing Unit – II. The acquisition was 
done to help the company in its forward integration and to expand its fabrication capabilities and to begin 
in-house galvanization. All the existing registrations, approvals and licences of such unit have been 
transferred from BSL Railtrack Engineers Private Limited to our company .

The acquisition was 
done to help the company in its forward integration and to expand its fabrication capabilities and to begin 
in-house galvanization. All the existing registrations, approvals and licences of such unit have been 
transferred from BSL Railtrack Engineers Private Limited to our company . The final approval in the form 
of factory license was transferred / re- issued in the name of our company on and it has now become 
operational. 
The integration of Manufacturing Unit -II will provide the Company with enhanced capabilities for better 
execution of orders, higher utilization of its existing manufacturing facilities, diversification of product 
offerings and addition of new customers, which are expected to increase the scale of operations. 
Accordingly, the Company anticipates higher inventory requirements and an increase in its overall working 
capital requirements to support the expanded operations. 
Due to the nature of our B2B operations, historically, the Company primarily operated with customers 
offering advance payments, instant payments, or payments through letters of credit. However, 
beginning Fiscal 2025, we have started engaging with new customers who typically operate on 
extended credit terms. While the credit risk associated with such customers remain minimal, the 
increase in the trade receivables cycle has resulted in delayed cash inflows. As in Fiscal 2026, Fiscal

Receivables 
Trade receivables represent amounts owed to the Company by its customers for 
the sale of goods in the ordinary course of business. Historically, the Company 
primarily catered to customers who made advance payments, instant payments, 
or payments through letters of credit, owing to limited working capital 
availability. Consequently, the Company maintained a low receivables cycle. 
However, beginning Fiscal 2025, in order to support business growth, expand 
its customer base, and increase market reach, the Company commenced offering 
credit facilities to customers in line with prevailing industry practices. As a result 
of this strategic shift, the trade receivables cycle increased from 3 days in Fiscal 
2024 and 45 days in Fiscal 2025 to 66 days in Fiscal 2026. 
 
Going forward, the Company expects to maintain a balanced mix of customer 
payment terms. Accordingly, the trade receivables period is estimated at 
approximately 63 days in Fiscal 2027 and is expected to stabilize at 
approximately 61 days in Fiscal 2028, in line with anticipated business volumes 
and improved working capital management.

Process and on the basis of quantitative and qualitative factors as described below. The face value of the Equity

times the face value at the higher end of the Price Band. Investors should refer to “Risk Factors”, “Our Business”,

Qualitative Factors 
 
Some of the qualitative factors which form the basis for computing the Issue Price are as follows: 
 
• Established track record of sound financial performance 
 
We have demonstrated a consistent track record of revenue growth, profitability and operational efficiency 
over the last three fiscals. Our revenue from operations has increased from ₹23,925.12 lakhs in Fiscal 2024 to 
₹33,956.36 lakhs in Fiscal 2025, and f urther to ₹ 44,401.61 lakhs in Fiscal 2026, representing a compound 
annual growth rate (“CAGR”) of approximately 36.23 %.

Our total income has also grown in line with this 
trend, from ₹23,980.68 lakhs in Fiscal 2024 to ₹34,066.82 lakhs in Fiscal 2025, and to ₹ 44,496.64 lakhs in 
Fiscal 2026 reflecting the consistent expansion of our business scale. 
 
• Focused Expertise in Structural Steel Products Manufacturing 
 
We are engaged in the business of manufacturing hot re-rolled structural steel products, primarily comprising 
Angles, Channels, MS Section, and Flats & Rods. Our focus on this product segment has enabled us to develop 
strong technical expertise in producti on processes, efficient inventory management practices, and a thorough 
understanding of customer requirements across applications and end- use industries. Over the years, this 
focused approach has allowed us to refine our operational capabilities and establ ish ourselves as a reliable 
manufacturer of structural steel products. 
 
• Strong Quality Systems Aligned with Indian and Global Standards 
 
All our products are manufactured in compliance with both Indian and international quality standards. We 
have implemented a well -defined quality control system that ensures close monitoring at every stage of 
production from the procurement of raw materials to the final inspection before dispatch. The Company also 
has an in-house Quality Control Room equipped for conducting necessary quality checks and inspections to 
monitor and ensure the quality and conformity of products at various stages of the manufacturing process. We 
are certified under ISO 9001:2015 (Quality Management System), Bureau of Indian Standards Licence No.

We 
are certified under ISO 9001:2015 (Quality Management System), Bureau of Indian Standards Licence No. 
CM/L-5900059318 along with the Indian Standard No. IS 2062:2011, ISO 14001:2015 (Environmental 
Management System), and ISO 45001:2018 (Occupational Health and Safety Management System). 
 
• Strategic location of Manufacturing Facilities 
 
As per CareEdge Report, our Manufacturing Unit I & II are strategically located in Durg District, Chhattisgarh, 
in close proximity to the Bhilai Steel Plant, one of India’s largest integrated steel producers, and within the 
mineral-rich eastern India belt. This strategic location provides the Company with efficient access to key raw 
materials, including steel and allied inputs, as well as proximity to major end- user industries such as 
infrastructure, power, railways, telecom, and engineering sectors.

• Well-positioned to take advantage of the growing demand 
 
As per the CareEdge Report, the Company is strategically positioned to benefit from the significant and 
sustained growth in India’s power transmission and railway electrification sectors. Over the past several 
decades, India’s power transmission network has expanded exponentially, reflecting consistent investments in 
high-voltage transmission infrastructure across central, state, and private ownership. The transmission network 
has grown from 34,000 circuit kilometres (Ckm) in 1980 to over 510,594 Ckm by FY27 This growth reflects 
sustained investments in high- voltage transmission lines across various voltage levels (220 kV to 800 kV), 
with notable additions in 765 kV and 400 kV categories under central and joint venture/private ownership. 
 
• Enhance Forward Integration and Synergy 
 
The Company has strengthened its business model by expanding in- house capabilities by entering into the 
manufacture and fabrication of engineered steel products through the acquisition of Manufacturing Unit II, in 
furtherance of the ATA dated September 12, 2025 and amended lease deed dated March 09, 2026. 
Manufacturing Unit II is equipped with in -house manufacturing, fabrication, engineering and galvanising 
facilities and enables the Company to undertake fabrication and engineering activities, as well as galvanising 
of steel products, in addition to its existing structural steel manufacturing operations.

Manufacturing Unit II is equipped with in -house manufacturing, fabrication, engineering and galvanising 
facilities and enables the Company to undertake fabrication and engineering activities, as well as galvanising

value chain of structural steel products, from procurement and processing of raw materials to manufacturing, 
fabrication, engineering, galvanising and delivery of finished steel products in accordance with customer 
specifications. The in-house galvanising facility facilitates value addition to the Company’s steel products by 
enhancing their corrosion resistance and durability, thereby enabling the Company to offer higher -value and 
more comprehensive steel solutions to its customers

A.1 Special Tax Benefits Available to the Company 
 
1. Concessional Tax Regime for Domestic Companies 
 
Under Section 115BAA of the Income-tax Act, 1961, a domestic company may opt to be taxed at a concessional 
rate of 22% on its total income, subject to fulfilment of the prescribed conditions, including restrictions relating 
to specified deductions, exemptions and set-off of certain losses and depreciation. 
The Company has exercised the option to be governed by the provisions of Section 115BAA of the Income -tax 
Act, 1961 with effect from Financial Year 2023–24.

taxed at the concessional rate of 22%, together with applicable surcharge and Health and Education Cess. At the 
currently applicable rates, the effective tax rate is approximately 25.17%, subject to the applicable provisions of 
the relevant Finance Act. 
 
With effect from 1 April 2026, the Income-tax Act, 2025 has replaced the Income-tax Act, 1961. The concessional 
tax regime available to domestic companies under Section 115BAA of the Income -tax Act, 1961 has been 
substantially carried forward under Section 200 of the Income-tax Act, 2025. Section 200 provides for taxation of 
eligible domestic companies at a concessional rate of 22%, subject to fulfilment of the prescribed conditions. The 
option exercised under the erstwhile Act is recognised under the corresponding provisions of the Income-tax Act, 
2025, subject to the applicable transitional provisions. 
 
Companies opting for the concessional regime under Section 200 are not subject to Minimum Alternate Tax 
("MAT") under Section 206 of the Income-tax Act, 2025, subject to the applicable provisions of law.

eligible assessee may claim a deduction of an amount equal to 30% of additional employee cost incurred in the 
course of its business in respect of eligible employees.

Global Steel Industry 
 
Overview of the Global Steel Industry 
 
Steel plays a pivotal role in construction and engineering, serving a wide range of industries 
including automotive, infrastructure, consumer goods, mechanical and medical equipment, 
packaging, and household utensils. Industry professionals consistently prefer steel as a building 
material due to its widespread availability, cost-effectiveness, strength, durability, ductility, and 
recyclability. According to the World Steel Association, manufacturers across the globe produce 
over 3,500 grades of steel, each offering distinct physical, chemical, and environmental properties 
tailored to specific applications. 
 
Global per capita steel consumption has declined steadily since CY21. By CY25, consumption 
dropped to 209 kg, down from 220 kg in CY23. This downward trend reflects a combination of 
cyclical and structural factors. The most significant driver has been the prolonged slowdown in 
China’s property and construction sector, which historically accounted for a substantial share of 
global steel consumption. As China’s urbanization and infrastructure build-out slow, steel 
intensity has moderated, reducing global demand growth. At the same time, weaker manufacturing 
activity in several developed economies, elevated interest rates, economic uncertainty and slower 
investment in construction have constrained steel consumption across major regions. Increased 
material efficiency, greater use of high-strength steels requiring lower volumes, and a gradual 
shift toward circular economy practices and scrap-based production have also reduced steel 
requirements per unit of economic output.

shift toward circular economy practices and scrap-based production have also reduced steel 
requirements per unit of economic output. Consequently, growth in emerging markets such as 
India has not been sufficient to fully offset the moderation in mature steel-consuming economies.

Global Production of Steel 
 
Global crude steel production grew at a compound annual growth rate (CAGR) of - 0.4% over the past six 
years, decreasing from 1,883 million tonnes (MT) in CY20 to 1,849 MT in CY25. Additionally, in the first 
seven months of CY26 (January– July), producers reduced output by 0.6% compared to the same period in 
CY25. This decline was primarily because reductions in a few large regions outweighed growth elsewhere. 
Global production fell year -on-year for the quarter, with Asia & Oceania down (driven mainly by China), 
along with declines in the EU and Russia/CIS/Ukraine and the Middle East. China was the biggest drag as

Overview of the Indian Steel Industry 
 
As of FY27 (April –June 2026, provisional), India's installed steel production capacity stood at 222 MTPA 
(Million Tonnes Per Annum). The country ranks as the second- largest consumer of finished steel, with 
consumption reaching 164 MT in FY26. This growth stems from the domestic availability of key raw materials 
such as iron ore, cost-effective labour, and strong demand from sectors like construction, consumer durables, 
capital goods, railways, real estate, and automobiles. Additionally, India’s extensive coastline has facilitated 
both exports and imports, positioning the country as a major player in the global steel industry. 
 
In CY25, India’s per capita finished steel consumption stood at 109.2 kg, well below the global average of 
209 kg.

both exports and imports, positioning the country as a major player in the global steel industry. 
 
In CY25, India’s per capita finished steel consumption stood at 109.2 kg, well below the global average of 
209 kg. To address this gap, the Government of India, under its Atmanirbhar Bharat vision, introduced the 
National Steel Policy 2017. The policy targets a steel-making capacity of 300 MT by CY30 and aims to raise 
per capita steel consumption to 160kg. These goals highlight the sector’s untapped domestic potential and its 
critical role in driving India’s future economic growth. India has attracted substantial investment into its steel 
sector through initiatives such as joint ventures and 100% foreign direct investment (FDI). These efforts have 
accelerated the industry's expansion and integration into global value chains.

Indian Re-rolled Structural Steel Products Market 
 
Overview 
 
By product, steel can be divided into long (non-flat) and flat products, both of which have either a hot-rolled, 
cold-formed, or coated surface. 
 
• Long (Non-Flat) Steel products: Long steel products encompass a variety of forms primarily used in 
construction, mechanical engineering, and energy sectors. Typically, available in straight lengths or 
custom-cut sizes, with wire rods being the exception, often wound in irregular coils, these products 
undergo shaping or sizing processes from hot -rolled or forged blooms, billets, or pencil ingots to 
achieve their final form. Different types of long products include bars & rods, CTD/TMT bars & 
rods, Wire rods, Angles, Shapes & Section, Rails, Wires, and bright bars for railways. These versatile 
materials offer durability and structural integrity, serving as essential components in various 
infrastructure projects and industrial applications worldwide. 
 
• Flat Steel products: Flat steel products are the result of processing slabs or thin slabs in rolling mills 
using flat rolls, offering versatility in applications across automotive and truck manufacturing, heavy 
machinery, construction, packaging, and appliances. These finishe d steel products, supplied in Hot 
Rolled (HR), Cold Rolled (CR), or coated conditions, cater to diverse needs.

decline in prices across key channel sections was attributable to a combination of elevated import volumes 
and global oversupply, particularly driven by aggressive exports from China, and subdued global demand, 
resulting in pricing pressure in the domestic market. The impact was more pronounced in the 75×40 mm and

declining to their lowest levels in December 2025.

MS Section 
 
MS section prices exhibited a relatively soft and range -bound trend during the period, with intermittent 
fluctuations reflecting changes in steel demand, raw material costs and market sentiment. Prices strengthened 
during the first half of 2024, supported by improving construction and infrastructure activity and firmer steel 
market conditions, but this momentum was not sustained. The subsequent moderation through the second half 
of 2024 and across 2025 indicates a period of subdued pricing, likely reflecting relatively balanced or uneven 
demand conditions and competitive pressure in the downstream steel market.

the year. This weakness may have been influenced by softer steel realisations, cautious buying by downstream 
consumers and fluctuations in input costs. For MS section manufacturers, such an environment can place 
pressure on gross margins, particularly where input costs remain elevated or price pass -through to customers 
is delayed. 
 
A recovery emerged during the first half of 2026, with prices improving sequentially across the March and 
June quarters. The recent uptrend indicates some strengthening in market conditions, potentially supported by 
improved infrastructure and construction demand, better steel market sentiment and stabilisation in raw

vi. Beams 
Pricing trends for steel beams reflect the broader cyclical movements observed in the domestic long and 
structural steel market. Prices typically respond to changes in steel demand, raw material costs, import 
availability and prevailing international steel prices. The Ministry of Steel has noted that the steel sector is 
deregulated, with prices of finished steel and key inputs such as iron ore and coking coal determined largely 
by market dynamics. Consequently, periods of weaker construction and industrial activity, together with softer 
input costs and higher import availability, can exert pressure on beam realizations. 
 
The domestic market has nevertheless continued to be supported by infrastructure and construction activity. 
The Ministry of Steel reported that finished steel consumption increased during FY2025 –26, supported by 
activity across infrastructure, construction , railways and manufacturing. This underlying demand provides 
support to structural steel products, including beams, although pricing momentum can remain uneven across 
product categories and dimensions. 
 
Import trends have also remained an important consideration for domestic steel pricing. Government data 
indicates that China accounted for a significant share of India’s finished steel imports during FY2023–24 and 
FY2024–25, highlighting continued exposure of domestic prices to international supply conditions. Policy 
measures aimed at protecting domestic steel producers from import-related pressures, including the safeguard 
duty imposed on certain steel products in April 2025, have subsequently supported a more favourable domestic 
pricing environment.

vii. Windmills 
 
Wind power in India is a mature and fast -growing end-user industry that converts a country’s wind resource 
into utility-scale electricity through the deployment of wind turbines, towers, foundations and balance-of-plant 
systems. As a generation sector it sits at the intersection of heavy engineering, civil construction and electrical 
systems requiring large component supply chains, predictable logistics and long-term service contracts. Policy 
support, auction mechanisms and grid-integration efforts have driven project development across coastal and 
inland wind belts, while manufacturers, EPC contractors and O&M providers form the core ecosystem.

211 
Steel products play a foundational role across that ecosystem. Long products such as pipes, tubulars, bars and 
structural sections are the primary material for towers, internal tower stiffeners, yaw and pitch shafts, and a 
range of forged components. Their mechanical strength, weldability and availability in tall lengths enable tall 
multi-section towers that reduce transportation complexity and provide the structural backbone for turbine 
assemblies. Flat products such as plates, sheets and strip are equally critical in nacelles, hubs, hubs’ cover 
plates, base plates for tower flanges, transformer tanks and cable trays. Precision cold -rolled strip is used 
where dimensional tolerance and surface finish matter, for example in electrical enclosures, grounding 
assemblies and certain bearing housings. Hot -rolled plates and heavy gauge sheets are preferred for welded 
structural items and foundation interface plates where toughness and weldability are priorities. 
 
Together, long and flat steels reduce complexity by standardizing fabrication practices, improving joint 
integrity, and simplifying maintenance and spare -parts logistics. Their recyclability and compatibility with 
domestic fabrication capacity also help keep project costs and lead times manageable. For steel producers, the 
wind sector presents steady demand for higher -specification grades and long -term supply agreements; for 
developers, reliable access to both long and flat steel is a key enabler of faster, more resilient wind projects.

viii. Refinery 
 
Refineries are capital -intensive, continuous -process industrial facilities that convert crude oils and other 
feedstocks into fuels, petrochemical feedstocks and specialty products. In India, the sector sits at the 
intersection of heavy mechanical engineering, metallurgy, civil works and process instrumentation demanding 
robust materials, precise fabrication and long-term operational reliability. Refineries require large volumes of 
pressure-containing equipment, extensive piping networks, storage tanks, heat -transfer surfaces and 
supporting steel structures, all of which must meet stringent safety, corrosion and metallurgical standards over 
multi-decade service lives. 
 
Long steel products (bars, sections, tubes and pipes) are the backbone of refinery mechanical systems. Pipes 
and tubulars form the arteries of a refinery carrying feedstock, intermediate streams and product flows between 
reactors, distillation columns, heat exchangers and storage. Structural sections, channels and rebar are essential 
for platforms, access structures, pipe- racks and foundations that support heavy equipment and enable safe 
maintenance. The availability of long lengths and high -strength grades reduces weld joints, shortens 
installation time, and improves structural integrity under cyclic loads and thermal expansion.

The availability of long lengths and high -strength grades reduces weld joints, shortens 
installation time, and improves structural integrity under cyclic loads and thermal expansion. Flat steel 
products (plates, sheets and strip) are equally vital for pressure vessels, column shells, jacketed reactors, heat-
exchanger shells, tank bottoms and flanges. Thick plates offer the toughness and weldability required for high-
pressure, high-temperature service; precision cold -rolled sheet and strip are used in cladding, enclosures and 
instrumentation panels where dimensional control matters. Clad plates and corrosion- resistant flat products 
permit combining a corrosion -resistant surface with a lower -cost structural backing, a cost -efficient solution 
in many refinery corrosive duties. 
 
Together, these steel products enable standardized fabrication, simplify spares inventory, and support modular 
construction approaches that shorten project schedules. For refinery operators, reliable domestic sourcing of 
specified steel grades reduces procurement risk and lifecycle costs; for fabricators, these product families 
improve weld quality, inspection throughput and long-term maintainability of critical process assets. 
 
ix. Renewable (Solar) 
 
India’s solar sector has emerged as a cornerstone of the country’s energy transition, a large, distributed, and 
fast-scaling end -user industry that spans project developers, module and tracker manufacturers, EPC 
contractors, financiers and long -term O&M pr oviders.

The technical scope ranges from utility- scale ground 
mount parks and hybrid farms to rooftop and off -grid systems, with government programmes and auctions 
steadily lowering costs and shortening execution timelines. India’s identified solar potenti al is roughly 748 
GW (NISE/MNRE estimate assuming 3% waste -land coverage). Policy support and active project

212 
commissioning have translated into robust additions. The current installed solar capacity stands at 164.59 GW 
as on 31st July 2026. 
 
Long and flat steel products are structural enablers across the solar value chain. Long products (tubulars, 
hollow sections, angles and channels) form trackers, pylons for elevated mounting, poles for small/mid- scale 
installations and the structural skeleton of ground- mount racking; their length, straightness and high- strength 
grades reduce on -site splices and erection time. Flat products (hot- rolled plates, cold -rolled sheets and 
precision strip) are used in module mounting plates, transformer and inverter enclosures, cable trays, junction 
boxes and foundation interface plates. 
 
Because many solar projects pursue modular, repeatable designs, consistent domestic supply of specified long 
and flat steel grades shortens lead times, simplifies logistics and reduces fabrication defects. Steel’s 
recyclability and long service life also h elp lifecycle cost and sustainability metrics for solar farms. 
Government schemes (solar parks, CPSU programmes and rooftop incentives) that stimulate rapid capacity 
addition thereby create predictable demand for both long and flat steel products.

x. Power 
 
India’s power sector is a large, capital -intensive end -user industry spanning generation, transmission, 
distribution and system operations. It supports heavy industry, services and households, and is evolving rapidly 
as renewables scale up alongside conventional plants. India’s total installed generation capacity reached about 
552 GW as of 31st July 2026, reflecting strong additions across technologies. Electricity output has also risen 
sharply along with expansion in national generation. 
 
This growth creates sustained demand for engineering, construction and long- lifecycle supply chains. Long 
steel products (structural sections, pipes, tubulars, rails and rebar) are fundamental: transmission towers, 
overhead line pylons, substation gantries, cable supports and the structural frames of switchyards rely on high-
strength long sections and tubulars that resist wind, seismic loads and fatigue while minimizing onsite welding 
and erection time. Flat steel products (plates, sheets and precision strip) are equally critical, used in transformer 
tanks, switchgear and control -room enclosures, busbars, base plates for foundations and welded pressure 
vessels in thermal and hydro plants where flatness, weldability and thick-plate toughness matter. 
 
Reliable domestic supply of specified long and flat steel grades shortens procurement lead times, standardizes 
fabrication, and reduces lifecycle maintenance risks.

Reliable domestic supply of specified long and flat steel grades shortens procurement lead times, standardizes 
fabrication, and reduces lifecycle maintenance risks. Expansion of grid capacity and reduction of transmission 
losses remain policy priorities as the system integrates more renewables; adequate, timely supply of both long 
and flat steels therefore underpins not just construction but long-term system resilience and operability. 
 
xi. Telecommunications 
 
India’s telecommunications industry is a vast, infrastructure -heavy end -user sector that underpins digital 
services, commerce and public administration. Active wireless (mobile) subscribers numbered about 1,282.38 
million in June 2026, reflecting the network scale and mass market reach of mobile services. 
 
The sector’s rapid modernization including dense 4G coverage and fast 5G rollout has driven higher data 
consumption, enterprise connectivity and new services such as fixed wireless access and IoT; TRAI’s yearly 
review highlights these continuing usage and service trends. 
 
Physical infrastructure remains the backbone of the sector: India had roughly 30.37 lakh base transceiver 
stations (BTS) as on 30 th June 2025, underscoring the scale of network infrastructure. By June 2026, around 
24,000 mobile towers had been commissioned under the DBN-funded 4G Saturation Project and other mobile 
projects. 5G BTS increased to 5,62,971, with 5G services available in 99.9% of districts.

213 
The Government is also supporting indigenous telecom technology through the TTDF, with 136 R&D projects 
and nearly Rs 543 crore of sanctioned funding as of June 2026, alongside the Rs 12,195 crore Telecom and 
Networking Products PLI scheme. 
 
Long and flat steel products are essential enablers for telecom infrastructure. Long products like lattice 
sections, hollow tubulars, angles, channels and threaded bars form towers, monopoles, rooftop masts and 
foundation anchors; their high- strength grades and long lengths reduce splices, speed erection and improve 
wind and fatigue-resistance. Flat steels like plates, sheets and strips are used for base plates, mounting brackets, 
cable trays, antenna mounting platforms, equipment racks and outdoor enclosur e panels where flatness, 
weldability and surface finish matter. Galvanised and weather -resistant coatings on both families extend 
service life in exposed telecom sites. Reliable, standardised domestic supply of specified long and flat steel 
grades shortens procurement cycles, reduces fabrication rework and supports rapid network expansion and 
maintenance. 
 
xii. Warehouses 
 
India’s warehousing sector is transitioning from ad- hoc storage to a strategic, asset -heavy industry driven by 
policy, multimodal connectivity and rising demand from manufacturing, 3PL and organised retail. The 
Government’s decision to grant the logistics (including warehousing and cold chain) sector infrastructure 
status has unlocked cheaper, longer-tenor financing and encouraged private investment.

The 
Government’s decision to grant the logistics (including warehousing and cold chain) sector infrastructure 
status has unlocked cheaper, longer-tenor financing and encouraged private investment. 
 
Multi-Modal Logistics Parks (MMLPs) and Free Trade & Warehousing Zones (FTWZs) are core policy levers: 
the government has approved 35 MMLP locations to improve freight efficiency, and MMLP development is 
being pushed with large capital allocations to build hub-and-spoke freight nodes. FTWZs (under the Foreign 
Trade/SEZ framework) further support export-oriented inventory handling and duty-deferred trade. 
 
From an operations standpoint, modern warehousing demands Grade-A buildings, mechanised handling, cold-
chain rooms and faster throughput, all of which increase the need for standardised structural systems and 
modular construction. That is where steel fits in: long steel products (rolled sections, hollow sections, tubulars 
and rails) form the structural skeleton frames for pre-engineered buildings, mezzanine floors, heavy-duty pallet 
racking, and crane rails delivering long- span capacity, high duty cycles and rapid on- site erection. Flat steel 
(plates, sheets and strip) is integral for roof and wall cladding, dock-level plates, conveyor supports, equipment 
bases, and prefabricated enclosures where dimensional flatness, weldability and surface finish matter. 
 
Galvanised long and flat steels extend life in exposed logistics yards and cold stores, reduce maintenance 
cycles, and simplify modular repairs and spares management.

Galvanised long and flat steels extend life in exposed logistics yards and cold stores, reduce maintenance 
cycles, and simplify modular repairs and spares management. As MMLPs, FTWZs and warehouse 
modernisation programmes roll out, predictable, long-term demand for specified long and flat steel grades will 
help fabricators standardise designs, shorten lead times and lower total cost of ownership for developers and 
occupiers. 
 
xiii. Construction 
 
India’s construction sector is a large, capital-intensive end-user industry spanning residential and commercial 
building, infrastructure (roads, bridges, ports, rail, airports), and specialised industrial projects. It supports 
employment, domestic steel an d cement demand, and urbanisation- driven services across value chains. The 
sector recorded a moderate performance in FY26 estimated to grow 7.1% for the year. 
 
Long and flat steel products are structural enablers across construction value chains. Long products such as 
rebars, structural sections (I-beams, channels, angles), hollow sections and rails form the skeleton of buildings, 
bridges, pre-engineered structures, pile cages and heavy -duty racking. Their high tensile strength, consistent 
straightness and availability in long lengths reduce splices, speed erection, and improve seismic and fatigue 
performance in tall and long -span structures. Flat steels such as h eavy plates, hot -rolled coils, cold -rolled

214 
sheets and precision strip are used for base plates, column and beam flange fabrication, bridge decks, shuttering 
plates, roofing and cladding, and equipment foundations where dimensional flatness and weldability matter. 
Thick plates are essential for heav y civil components (bridge bearings, gantry supports) while thinner cold -
rolled sheets serve facades, doors and interior systems. 
 
Galvanised and coated long/flat steels extend service life, lower maintenance in exposed environments, and

Galvanized Structural Steel Products 
 
Galvanized structural steel products are steel products coated with a layer of zinc to improve corrosion 
resistance and extend service life, particularly in applications exposed to moisture, outdoor conditions and 
corrosive environments. Galvanizing is widely used for structural steel components where durability and 
relatively low maintenance requirements are important considerations. 
 
The galvanizing process generally involves preparation of the steel surface, followed by application of a zinc 
coating. In the case of Hot -dip galvanizing (HDG) , fabricated steel components are immersed in a bath of 
molten zinc, allowing the zinc to bond metallurgically with the steel surface. Electro -galvanizing uses an 
electrochemical process to deposit a comparatively thinner and more uniform zinc coating. HDG is generally 
more suited to structural and outdoor applications requiring higher corrosion protection, while electro -
galvanized products are used where surface finish and dimensional precision are more relevant. 
 
The market for galvanized steel can broadly be segmented by type, including hot -dip and electro-galvanized 
steel, and by product, comprising structures, pipes and tubes, sheets and strips, and other products. Structural 
applications include components used in railways, solar projects and transmission infrastructure, where 
protection against corrosion can support longer operating life.

217 
Fabrication forms an important intermediate stage for galvanized structural products. Steel sections, 
plates and other components are cut, bent, drilled, welded and assembled to the required specifications before 
galvanizing, particularly where the end product comprises fabricated structures. Depending on the application, 
fabrication may therefore precede the galvanizing stage, with appropriate design and process controls required 
to ensure adequate coating coverage. In some applications, galvanized steel products may subsequently 
undergo additional assembly or finishing before being supplied to the end user. 
 
Zinc is the principal raw material used in the galvanizing process. Accordingly, the availability and pricing of 
zinc have a bearing on the cost structure of galvanized products. The assessment of the zinc value chain would 
include domestic production, imports and exports, and price movements. 
 
Demand for galvanized structural steel is supported by applications in railways, solar energy and transmission 
towers, where infrastructure expansion, outdoor exposure and requirements for durable structures contribute 
to the use of corrosion-resistant steel products. Overall, the market is influenced by infrastructure investment, 
project activity, steel and zinc prices, fabrication requirements and the adoption of corrosion- resistant 
materials across end-user industries.

Production Linked Incentive (PLI) Scheme 
• India’s Production Linked Incentive Scheme for Specialty Steel, launched in July 2021 with an outlay of 
Rs 63.22 billion, is designed to deepen domestic manufacturing capabilities, accelerate technology 
adoption and reduce import dependence in high- value steel grades critical to automobiles, defence, 
railways, aerospace, power, renewable energy and corrosion - or heat-resistant tubes and pipes. Covering 
coated and plated steel, high -strength and wear -resistant steel, specialty rails, alloy steel products and 
wires, and electrical steel, the scheme initially targeted an increase in specialty steel production from 17.6 
million tonnes in FY20 to 42.2 million tonnes by FY27, alongside investment mobilisation of about Rs 
396.25 billion by FY30.

• Its subsequent iterations have progressively widened participation: PLI 1.1, launched on January 6, 2025 
for FY26 to FY30, relaxed investment and capacity thresholds, introduced production carry- forward 
flexibility and lowered entry requirements for strate gically important CRGO steel; while Round 1.2, 
launched on November 4, 2025, expanded coverage to 22 subcategories, including superalloys, stainless 
steel, alloy forgings, titanium alloys and coated steels, offering incentives of 4% to 15% on incremental 
sales and adopting FY25 as the revised base year. 
 
• With earlier rounds attracting committed investments of Rs 438.74 billion, the evolving framework reflects 
a targeted industrial strategy to create advanced capacity, encourage process innovation, substitute imports, 
strengthen export competitiveness and position India as a global hub for high -value specialty steel 
manufacturing. 
 
 
Domestically Manufactured Iron & Steel Products (DMI&SP): 
• The Domestically Manufactured Iron and Steel Products (DMI&SP) Policy, approved on May 8, 2017, 
provides preference in government procurement to iron and steel products manufactured by India -
registered entities, including units in Special Economic Zones, subject to prescribed domestic value 
addition. The qualifying threshold, initially set at 15% to 50%, was revised to 20% to 50% under the 
policy dated December 31, 2020.

The qualifying threshold, initially set at 15% to 50%, was revised to 20% to 50% under the 
policy dated December 31, 2020. 
 
• Intended to stimulate domestic steel production and consumption, improve capacity utilisation and 
promote import substitution, the policy has been periodically extended, including for six months from 
May 29, 2024. Under the revised policy dated December 17, 2025, its validity has been extended to March 
31, 2027, while its coverage has been broadened across Central Ministries, central public- sector 
enterprises and government-controlled entities, including steel-intensive infrastructure procurement. 
 
• The revised framework also mandates manufacturer registration on a designated government portal, 
supported by self-certification, periodic audits and stronger enforcement provisions, including penalties 
and deregistration for misdeclaration or non- compliance, thereby transforming domestic procurement 
preference into a more transparent and accountable mechanism for strengthening India’s steel -
manufacturing ecosystem. 
 
Quality Control Order on Steel: 
• The Ministry of Steel has introduced a Steel Quality Control Order (QCO), thereby banning sub-
standard/defective steel products from the domestic market alongside imports to ensure the availability of 
quality steel to the industry, users, and the public at large. 
 
• This measure is being taken to enhance the availability of quality steel to the users. According to the 
Order, it is ensured that only quality steel conforming to the relevant BIS standards is made available to

235 
the end users. BIS (Bureau of Indian Standards) Certification is a quality assurance process that ensures 
products meet Indian standards, verifying their quality, safety, and reliability. While BIS certification is 
voluntary for many products, it is mandatory for specific items, including certain steel products like TMT 
bars, to ensure public safety and compliance with Indian Standards. Certified products bear the ISI mark, 
indicating adherence to prescribed quality standards. The certification is typically valid for one to two 
years and can be renewed if the product and standards remain unchanged. 
 
• As of August 2024, the QCO covers 151 categories of steel and steel products including carbon steel, 
alloy steel, and stainless steel. In addition, goods & articles made up of steel such as stainless -steel pipe 
& tubes, laminations/ cores of transformers, products of tin plate & tin-free steel, etc., have been notified 
to prevent circumvention of the Steel Quality Control Order. 
 
• Through the Steel and Steel Products (Quality Control) Amendment Order, 2025, notified on 20 
November 2025, the Ministry of Steel has temporarily deferred mandatory BIS enforcement for selected 
steel and steel product categories (for 1 year or 3 years, depending on the product) to allow industry time 
to comply, while retaining the core QCO framework covering 151 BIS notified standards, including the 
requirement that both finished steel and critical intermediate inputs must conform to BIS standards once 
enforcement becomes operative.

India’s Carbon Emission Reduction Targets: 
 
At COP30, India reaffirmed a climate -action strategy grounded in equity, national circumstances and the 
principle of Common but Differentiated Responsibilities and Respective Capabilities (CBDR-RC), calling for 
a shift from commitments to credible implemen tation. India emphasised that developing economies require 
predictable, adequate and concessional climate finance, alongside affordable technology access, to reconcile 
low-carbon transition with development imperatives such as rapid energy-demand growth and continued coal 
dependence. Highlighting its progress in expanding renewable energy and forest cover and reducing the 
emissions intensity of GDP, India reiterated its targets of achieving 500 GW of non-fossil-fuel power capacity 
and reducing GDP emissions intensity by 45% from 2005 levels by 2030, followed by net -zero emissions by 
2070, supported by initiatives in green hydrogen, biofuels, renewable power and nuclear energy. By 
positioning COP30 as a “COP of Implementation and Delivery on Promises,” India placed adaptation, 
resilience and a people- centric just transition at the centre of the global agenda, arguing that stronger 
international cooperation and fulfilment of developed- country financing commitments are essential for 
climate-resilient growth across the developing world.

• Threat of New Entrants

• Bargaining Power of Suppliers 
 
Moderate to low 
• Inputs like billets and scrap are sourced from multiple suppliers. 
• Companies with bulk purchase agreements and MoUs with suppliers, enjoy steady supply and some 
price advantage. 
• Since steel supply is currently higher than demand, Bulk buyers are at an advantage. 
• Businesses with minimum or partial backward integration, leverage its purchase scale and reliable 
credit history to bargain with the suppliers. 
Result: Raw material prices remain volatile, but mid-size operators can be flexible to take advantage of market 
dynamics.

Low to moderate

Switching costs are high because of compliance and risk factors. 
o Large EPCs and government buyers still negotiate aggressively, especially in tenders. 
o Fast delivery, custom dimensions, and technical support add value beyond pricing. 
Result: Buyers have some price influence in tenders, but their ability to replace existing suppliers is limited.

Industry Production Process 
 
 
• Iron Ore to Billets 
o Iron ore is mined from the earth and is one of the main raw materials.

240 
o The mined iron is transported to a plant and converted into billets, which are rectangular 
bars of metal. 
 
• Billet Processing Steps 
o Billet Yard: Billets are stored in a large yard. 
o Reheating Furnace: Billets are heated to make them soft and easier to work with. 
o Descaler: Hot billets go through a machine that removes scale (oxide layer) from their surface. 
o Roughing Stand: Billets are pressed and shaped roughly. 
 
• Shaping and Finishing 
o Cropping Shear: Unwanted ends or portions of the billet are cut off. 
o Finishing Stand: The material is further shaped into more precise sizes and forms. 
o Straightened Machine: The shaped product is made straight and even. 
 
• Cutting, Stacking, and Final Processing 
o Cutting Mechanism: Finished steel is cut to desired lengths. 
o Stacker: The cut pieces are stacked neatly. 
o Strapping Machine: Bundles of steel are strapped together for shipping. 
o Collecting Bay: Finished bundles are collected and prepared for delivery. 
 
• Steel Products Creation 
o After all these steps, the steel is ready to be turned into different products such as angles, 
channels, flats, and rods, which are used in construction and manufacturing.This process takes 
raw iron and turns it into useful steel pieces through heating, shaping, cutting, and finishing.

Manufacturing Process 
 
(1) Process for making Structural Steel Products 
 
 
1. Raw Material Procurement and Storage 
 
The primary raw materials, billets and blooms, are sourced from various suppliers and stored in the 
manufacturing facility. On receipt, a sample is drawn from each lot and subjected to laboratory testing to

266 
check its chemical composition and mechanical properties. A quality report is then generated, and only 
material meeting the required standards is taken forward for production. 
 
2. Cutting and Reheating 
 
Based on the production plan, billets are cut to the required size and placed on conveyor belts leading to 
the reheating furnace. The billets are then uniformly heated to a temperature of around 1200°C, making 
them malleable for the rolling process. 
 
3. Descaling and Rolling 
 
Once heated, the billets pass through a descaler, where surface impurities and oxide scales formed during 
heating are removed with the help of a steel plank. The billets then move to the rolling stands, where they 
undergo multiple passes through rollers. T his stage reduces the cross -section and progressively shapes 
the billets into the desired size and profile. 
 
4. Precision Rolling 
 
This stage ensures precise control over dimensions, sectional geometry, and surface finish of the final 
product. Continuous monitoring and adjustments during rolling enable the achievement of specified 
tolerances, uniform mechanical properties, and consistent quality in accordance with applicable standards 
and customer specifications. 
 
5. Cooling and Cutting 
 
After achieving the required profile and dimensional accuracy, the rolled products are subjected to a 
controlled cooling process, which allows the material to attain the desired mechanical properties, 
dimensional stability, and surface finish. Thereafter, the cooled products are cut into specific lengths 
using a hot saw, as per customer requirements or internal specifications.

6. Finishing & Quality Checks 
 
The straightened products are collected in the bay and systematically stacked. Before dispatch, a Final 
Quality Control Inspection is carried out. Samples from the finished lots are tested for physical and 
mechanical properties, including tensile strength, bend, and impact resistance. Only after successful 
clearance are the products approved for dispatch to customers. 
 
(2) Fabrication Process for Manufacturing Engineered Products 
 
Based on specific customer or project requirements, the finished structural steel products may be further 
processed through fabrication. Fabrication is the process of converting re -rolled structural steel products such 
as Angles, Channels, and MS Sections into customised shapes, dimensions, and assemblies as per customer 
specifications. While our current in -house fabrication activities are limited to straightening and cutting, the 
Company undertakes cutting of re-rolled steel products, such as angles and channels, into the required sizes in 
accordance with the job card or cutting plan issued for the respective order. From the current Fiscal, the 
Company is licensed to undertake the fabrication process at Manufacturing Unit II. The key stages of 
fabrication are as follows: 
 
1. Straightening and Cutting 
 
In the initial stage, re-rolled products such as angles or channels are cut into the required sizes based on 
the job card or cutting plan issued for a particular order. Cutting operations are carried out using cutting

267 
machine, depending on the thickness of the material and the dimensional accuracy required. This process 
ensures that the steel sections conform precisely to the specified dimensions for further fabrication. 
 
2. Punching 
 
Following cutting, holes are created on the steel sections to facilitate assembly and joining. Punching is 
carried out using hydraulic or mechanical punching machines equipped with dies to achieve precise hole 
placement. For thicker sections or where speci fic requirements exist. This step plays a vital role in 
ensuring that fabricated components can be securely bolted or fastened during assembly. 
 
3. Marking 
 
Once punching is complete, marking is undertaken in accordance with the unique design plan mentioned 
in the job card. Marking serves as a guide for subsequent fabrication processes such as bending or 
notching and ensures proper alignment with design and assembly specifications. This step is essential for 
maintaining accuracy and avoiding deviations in the final product. 
 
4. Notching 
 
Notching involves the removal of small sections from steel angles and channels to enable proper fitting 
in joints or assemblies. Using notching machines, this process is used for cutting the edges which 
facilitates precise joining as per the drawing plan. Accurate notching is critical for ensuring both 
dimensional correctness and structural stability of the final assembly. 
 
5. Intermediate Inspection 
 
At this stage, an intermediate inspection is conducted after cutting, punching, marking, and notching.

Accurate notching is critical for ensuring both 
dimensional correctness and structural stability of the final assembly. 
 
5. Intermediate Inspection 
 
At this stage, an intermediate inspection is conducted after cutting, punching, marking, and notching. 
This inspection ensures that the semi -fabricated sections conform to the job card and drawing 
specifications before proceeding to subsequent stages of processing. 
 
6. Heating and Bending 
 
In cases where shaping or curving of steel is required, the sections are heated. Once adequately heated, 
bending is carried out using hydraulic presses or bending machines to achieve the desired shape. To 
correct dimensional changes caused by thermal expan sion, the heated material is further processed 
through power pass machines, ensuring accuracy and uniformity of the finished shape. 
 
7. Inspection 
 
Upon completion of fabrication, the product undergoes a final inspection to verify conformity with the 
job card and design plan. Key parameters such as dimensional accuracy, hole positioning, notching 
quality and overall finish are thoroughly checked. Only after successful inspection are the products 
cleared for dispatch. 
 
(3) Galvanization Process for making Engineered Products 
 
The Company has been engaged in manufacturing of galvanizing of steel products and has obtained the 
requisite licence to commence the manufacturing of galvanised steel products from the current Fiscal, wherein 
steel products are coated with a protective layer of zinc to enhance their resistance to corrosion and improve 
their durability.

The galvanized products are intended for applications across power, renewable energy, 
transmission and other sectors where enhanced corrosion protection and service life are required. From the 
current Fiscal, the Company is licensed to undertake the fabri cation process at Manufacturing Unit II. As per

268 
the CareEdge Report, demand for galvanized structural steel products is expected to remain strong, driven by 
their increasing use in corrosion- prone applications across power transmission, renewable energy and 
infrastructure projects, supporting our entry into galvanizing as part of our forward- integration strategy. The 
key stages of the galvanization process are as follows: 
 
i. Surface Preparation 
 
The steel products are initially subjected to surface preparation to remove dirt, oil, grease, rust and other 
contaminants from the surface. Proper surface preparation is essential to ensure effective adhesion and 
uniformity of the zinc coating. 
 
ii. Degreasing 
 
The steel products are immersed in a degreasing solution to remove oil, grease and other organic 
contaminants present on the surface. This ensures that the surface is adequately cleaned before further 
treatment. 
 
iii. Pickling 
 
Following degreasing, the steel products are treated with an acidic solution to remove rust, mill scale and 
other oxides from the surface. Pickling results in a clean and chemically active steel surface suitable for 
subsequent galvanizing. 
 
iv. Fluxing 
 
The cleaned steel products are subjected to fluxing, wherein a flux solution is applied to prevent oxidation 
of the prepared steel surface and facilitate proper bonding between the steel and molten zinc during the 
galvanizing process.

iv. Fluxing 
 
The cleaned steel products are subjected to fluxing, wherein a flux solution is applied to prevent oxidation 
of the prepared steel surface and facilitate proper bonding between the steel and molten zinc during the 
galvanizing process. 
 
v. Drying and Pre-heating 
 
After fluxing, the steel products are dried and, where required, pre -heated prior to immersion in the 
molten zinc bath. This stage helps minimise moisture and ensures appropriate conditions for the 
galvanizing process. 
 
vi. Hot-Dip Galvanizing 
 
The prepared steel products are immersed in a bath of molten zinc maintained at the required operating 
temperature. During immersion, a metallurgical reaction takes place between the steel and molten zinc, 
resulting in the formation of zinc -iron alloy laye rs with an outer layer of zinc, thereby providing 
protection against corrosion. 
 
vii. Withdrawal and Cooling 
 
After achieving the required coating, the steel products are withdrawn from the molten zinc bath at a 
controlled rate to facilitate uniform coating. Excess zinc is removed, where required, and the galvanized 
products are subsequently cooled and allowed to solidify. 
 
viii. Final Inspection 
 
Upon completion of galvanization, the products undergo final inspection to verify the quality and 
uniformity of the zinc coating. Parameters such as coating appearance, coverage, adhesion and coating

269 
thickness are checked, as applicable, against the relevant specifications and customer requirements. 
Products conforming to the specified quality requirements are cleared for dispatch.

As per the CareEdge Report, our Manufacturing Unit I & II are located in the mineral rich belt of Chhattisgarh,

generally borne by our distributors and direct customers.

Bureau of Indian Standards Act, 2016 (“BIS Act”) 
 
The BIS Act provides for the establishment of the Bureau of Indian Standards (“ BIS”) for the harmonious 
development of the activities of standardization, conformity assessment and quality assurance of goods, articles, 
processes, systems and services. The functions of the BIS, under the BIS Act includes, among others, (a) 
recognizing as an Indian standard, any standard established for any article or process by any other institution in 
India or elsewhere; (b) enter and search places, premises or vehicles, and inspect and seize goods, articles and 
documents to enforce the provisions of the BIS Act; (c) undertake testing of samples for purposes other than for 
conformity assessment; and (d) undertake activities related to legal metrology. The BIS Act empowers the Central 
Government in consultation with the BIS to order compulsory use of standard mark for any goods or process if it 
finds it expedient to do so in public interest. The BIS Act also provides penalties in case there is a contravention 
of the provisions of the BIS Act.

The Electricity Act provides for, inter alia, generation, transmission, distribution, trading and use of electricity. It 
governs the establishment, operation and maintenance of any electricity generating company and prescribes 
technical standards in relation to the connectivity of generating companies with the grid. As per the provisions of 
the Electricity Act, generating companies are required to establish, operate and maintain generating stations, 
substations and dedicated transmission lines. As per the provisions of the Electricity Act, the generating 
companies are required to establish, operate and maintain generating stations, tie-lines, sub-stations and dedicated 
transmission lines. Further, the generating company may supply electricity to any licensee or even directly to 
consumers, subject to availing open access to the transmission and distribution systems and payment of 
transmission charges, including wheeling charges and any other open access charges, as may be determined by 
the relevant electricity regulatory commission. In terms of the Electricity Act, open access means the non -
discriminatory provision for the use of transmission lines or distribution system or associated facilities with such 
lines or system, by any licensee or consumer or a person engaged in generation in accordance with the regulations 
specified by the relevant electricity regulatory commission.

Under the Electricity Act, the transmission, distribution and trade of electricity are regulated activities that require 
licenses from the Central Electricity Regulatory Commission (“ CERC”), the concerned State Electricity 
Regulatory Commissions (“SERCs”) or a joint commission (constituted by an agreement entered into by two or 
more state governments or the central government in relation to one or more state governments, as the case may 
be). However, in accordance with Section 7 of the Electricity Act, a generating company may establish, operate 
and maintain a generating station without obtaining a license under the Electricity Act if it complies with the 
technical standards relating to connectivity with the grid prescribed under clause (b) of Section 73 of the Electricity 
Act. Under Section 86 of the Electricity Act, the SERCs are required to promote co -generation and generation of 
electricity from renewable sources of energy by providing suitable measures for connectivity with the grid and 
sale of electricity to any person from sources other than the incumbent distribution licensee under the provision 
of open access. 
 
Additionally, the Electricity Rules, 2005 (the “ Electricity Rules ”) also prescribe a regulatory framework for 
developing captive generating plants. Pursuant to the Electricity Rules, a power plant shall qualify as a captive 
power plant only if not less than 26% of ownership is held by captive users and not less than 51% of the aggregate 
electricity generated in such plant, determined on an annual basis, is consumed for captive use.

In case of a 
generating station owned by a company formed as a special purpose vehicle, the equity shares of such special 
purpose vehicle required to be held by the captive user(s) are to be determined with reference to such unit or units 
identified for captive use and not with reference to the generating station as a whole, and the electricity required 
to be consumed by the captive user(s) mus t not be less than 26% of the proportionate equity interest of the 
Company related to the generating unit or units identified as the captive generating plant.

of any of the provisions of the Environment Protection Act or the EP Rules framed thereunder, the punishment includes

Code on Wages, 2019 
 
This Code received the assent of the President of India on August 8, 2019, and subsumes four existing laws 
namely, the Payment of Wages Act, 1936, the Minimum Wages Act, 1948, the Payment of Bonus Act, 1965 and 
the Equal Remuneration Act, 1976. The Central Government vide notification dated December 18, 2020, notified 
certain provisions of the Code on Wages, mainly in relation to the constitution of the advisory board. The 
remaining provisions of this Code have been brought into force with effect from November 21, 2025. It regulates, 
inter alia, the minimum wages payable to employees, the manner of payment and calculation of wages and the 
payment of bonus to employees. Its primary objective is to create a uniform and streamlined framework for wage-
related regulations across all sectors of employment. A key feature of the Code is the universalization of minimum 
wage and timely wage payment provisions, making them applicable to all employees, including those in the 
unorganized sector, thereby removing previous wage ceilings and employment -specific limitations.

A key feature of the Code is the universalization of minimum 
wage and timely wage payment provisions, making them applicable to all employees, including those in the 
unorganized sector, thereby removing previous wage ceilings and employment -specific limitations. The Code 
introduces the concept of a national "floor wage" to be determined by the Central Government, which will serve 
as a baseline that state- level minimum wages cannot fall below. Furthermore, it prohibits gender discrimination 
in matters of wages and recruitment for the same or similar nature of work, codifies the rules for annual bonus 
payments, and specifies clear timelines for wage payments and permissible deductions. The enforcement 
mechanism is al so revamped, introducing the role of an "Inspector -cum-Facilitator" to advise employers and 
employees, alongside traditional inspection functions, aiming for a more transparent and less adversarial 
compliance system. 
 
Industrial Relations Code, 2020 
 
This Code received the assent of the President of India on September 28, 2020, and it subsumes three existing 
legislations, namely, the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, the Trade Unions Act, 1926 and the Industrial Employment 
(Standing Orders) Act, 1946. The provisions of this Code have been brought into force with effect from November 
21, 2025.

The provisions of this Code have been brought into force with effect from November 
21, 2025. It significantly increases operational flexibility for companies by raising the employee threshold from 
100 to 300 for requiring prior government permission for layof fs, retrenchment, and closure, and for mandating 
formal standing orders. While providing this flexibility, the Code also introduces several worker -centric 
provisions, including an expanded definition of 'worker,' the formal recognition of fixed- term employment with 
pro-rata benefits, and the establishment of a 'Reskilling Fund' for retrenched employees. Furthermore, it 
establishes a clear framework for recognizing a sole negotiating union to streamline collective bargaining and 
imposes stricter conditions, such as a mandatory notice period, for strikes and lock- outs, aiming to balance 
employer flexibility with industrial harmony.

outside the traditional safety net. The Code establishes a framewo rk for this expansion through the mandatory 
registration of all workers on a national portal and the creation of a dedicated Social Security Fund to finance 
schemes for them.

Tax Identification Number (GSTIN). In case a person has multiple business verticals in multiple locations in a 
state, a separate application will be made for registrat ion of each and every location. The registered assessee is

Short Term Employee Benefit obligation:

I. Defined Contribution plans:

contributions are recognised as employee benefit expense when they are due.
II. Gratuity Obligation
The liability or asset recognised in the balance sheet in respect of gratuity plans is the present value of the defined benefit obligation at the
end of the reporting period less the fair value of plan assets.

II. Gratuity Obligation
The liability or asset recognised in the balance sheet in respect of gratuity plans is the present value of the defined benefit obligation at the
end of the reporting period less the fair value of plan assets. The defined benefit obligation is calculated annually by actuaries using the
projected unit credit method. 
The present value of the defined benefit obligation is determined by discounting the estimated future cash outflows by reference to market
yields at the end of the reporting period on government bonds that have terms approximating to the terms of the related obligation. 
The net interest cost is calculated by applying the discount rate to the net balance of the defined benefit obligation and the fair value of plan
assets. This cost is included in employee benefit expense in the statement of profit and loss. 
Remeasurement gains and losses arising from experience adjustments and changes in actuarial assumptions are recognised in the period in
which they occur, directly in other comprehensive income. 
Changes in the present value of the defined benefit obligation resulting from plan amendments or curtailments are recognised immediately
in profit and loss as past service cost.

Annexure V - Material Accounting Policies to the restated financial statements
Material Accounting Policies and explanatory notes to Financial Information
(q) Lease Accounting
Assets taken on lease:
The Company mainly has lease arrangements for land taken for its Factory.
The Company assesses whether a contract is or contains a lease, at inception of a contract. The assessment involves the exercise of
judgement about whether (i) the contract involves the use of an identified asset, (ii) the Company has substantially all of the economic
benefits from the use of the asset through the period of the lease, and (iii) the Company has the right to direct the use of the asset.
The Company recognises a right-of-use asset (“ROU”) and a corresponding lease liability at the lease commencement date. The ROU asset
is initially recognised at cost, which comprises the initial amount of the lease liability adjusted for any lease payments made at or before the
commencement date, plus any initial direct costs incurred and an estimate of costs to dismantle and remove the underlying asset or to restore
the underlying asset or the site on which it is located, less any lease incentives. They are subsequently measured at cost less accumulated
depreciation and impairment losses.

They are subsequently measured at cost less accumulated
depreciation and impairment losses.
The ROU asset is depreciated using the straightline method from the commencement date to the earlier of, the end of the useful life of the
ROU asset or the end of the lease term. If a lease transfers ownership of the underlying asset or the cost of the ROU asset reflects that the
Company expects to exercise a purchase option, the related ROU asset is depreciated over the useful life of the underlying asset. The
estimated useful lives of ROU assets are determined on the same basis as those of property and equipment. In addition, the right-of-use asset
is periodically reduced by impairment losses, if any, and adjusted for certain re-measurements of the lease liability.
The lease liability is initially measured at the present value of the lease payments that are not paid at the commencement date, discounted
using the interest rate implicit in the lease or, if that rate cannot be readily determined, the Company uses an incremental borrowing rate
specific to the Company, term and currency of the contract. Generally, the Company uses its incremental borrowing rate as the discount rate.
Lease payments included in the measurement of the lease liability include fixed payments, variable lease payments that depend on an index
or a rate known at the commencement date; and extension option payments or purchase options payment which the Company is reasonable
certain to exercise. 
Variable lease payments that do not depend on an index or rate are not included in the measurement the lease liability and the ROU asset.

Variable lease payments that do not depend on an index or rate are not included in the measurement the lease liability and the ROU asset.
The related payments are recognised as an expense in the period in which the event or condition that triggers those payments occurs and are
included in the line “other expenses” in the statement of profit or loss.
After the commencement date, the amount of lease liabilities is increased to reflect the accretion of interest and reduced for the lease
payments made and remeasured (with a corresponding adjustment to the related ROU asset) when there is a change in future lease payments
in case of renegotiation, changes of an index or rate or in case of reassessment of options.
Under previous GAAP, interest free security deposits (that are refundable in cash on completion of the term) are recorded at their
transaction value. Under Ind AS, all financial assets are required to be recognised initially at fair value. Accordingly, the Company has fair
valued these security deposits under Ind AS and subsequently measured at amortised cost.
Short-term leases and leases of low-value assets:
The Company has elected not to recognize ROU assets and lease liabilities for short term leases as well as low value assets and recognizes
the lease payments associated with these leases as an expense in the statement of profit and loss.
(r) Exceptional Items
An ordinary item of income or expense which by its size, nature, occurrence or incidence requires a disclosure in order to improve
understanding of the performance of the Company is treated as an exceptional item in the Statement of Profit and loss.

The Company has recognised a lease liability measured at the present value of the remaining lease payments, and right-of-use (ROU) asset at an amount equal to
lease liability (adjusted for any related prepayments). Management has exercised judgement in determining whether extension and termination options are
reasonably certain to be exercised. The Company has measured its lease liability at amortised cost using the effective interest method. The Company uses its
incremental borrowing rate as the discount rate. Lease liability on short-term leases and low-value assets is not created.
The Company does not face a significant liquidity risk with regard to its lease liabilities as the current assets are sufficient to meet the obligations related to lease
liabilities as and when they fall due. The Company’s lease asset classes primarily consist of leases for land. The Company assesses whether a contract contains a
lease, at inception of a contract. A contract is, or contains, a lease if the contract conveys the right to control the use of an identified asset for a period of time in
exchange of consideration. To assess whether a contract conveys the right to control the use of an identified asset, the Company assesses whether: (i) the contract
involves the use of an identified asset (ii) the Company has substantially all the economic benefits from the use of the asset through the period of the lease and (iii)
the Company has the right to direct the use of the asset.

At the date of commencement of the lease, the Company recognizes a right-of-use asset (“ROU”) and a corresponding lease liability for all lease arrangements in
which it is a lessee, except for leases with a term of twelve months or less (short-term leases) and low value leases. For these short-term and low value leases, the
Company recognizes the lease payments as an operating expense in the statement of profit and loss. 
Certain lease arrangements include the options to extend or terminate the lease before the end of the lease term. ROU assets and lease liabilities include the options
when it is reasonably certain that they will be exercised.
The lease liability is initially measure at amortized cost at the present value of the future lease payments. The lease payments are discounted using the interest rate
implicit in the lease or, if not readily determinable, using the incremental borrowing rates in the country of domicile of these leases. Lease liabilities are remeasured
with a corresponding adjustment to the related right of use asset if the Company changes its assessment if whether it will exercise an extension or a termination
option.

Characteristics of defined benefit plans
The entity has a defined benefit gratuity plan in India (funded). The entity’s defined benefit gratuity plan is a final salary plan for employees, which
requires contributions to be made to a separately administered fund maintained under a group gratuity insurance policy with SBI Life Insurance Company
Limited.
The plan assets are administered by SBI Life Insurance Company Limited in accordance with the terms and conditions of the insurance policy. The entity is
responsible for making contributions to the policy in accordance with the terms of the gratuity plan.
Gratuity is a defined benefit plan and entity is exposed to the Following Risks:
Interest rate risk: A fall in the discount rate which is linked to the G.Sec. Rate will increase the present value of the liability requiring higher provision. A
fall in the discount rate generally increases the mark to market value of the assets depending on the duration of asset.
Salary Risk: The present value of the defined benefit plan liability is calculated by reference to the future salaries of members.

A
fall in the discount rate generally increases the mark to market value of the assets depending on the duration of asset.
Salary Risk: The present value of the defined benefit plan liability is calculated by reference to the future salaries of members. As such, an increase in the
salary of the members more than assumed level will increase the plan's liability.
Investment Risk: The present value of the defined benefit plan liability is calculated using a discount rate which is determined by reference to market yields
at the end of the reporting period on government bonds. If the return on plan asset is below this rate, it will create a plan deficit. Currently, for the plan in
India, it has a relatively balanced mix of investments in government securities, and other debt instruments.
Asset Liability Matching Risk: The plan faces the ALM risk as to the matching cash flow. Since the plan is invested in lines of Rule 101 of Income Tax
Rules, 1962, this generally reduces ALM risk.
Mortality risk: Since the benefits under the plan is not payable for life time and payable till retirement age only, plan does not have any longevity risk.
Concentration Risk: Plan is having a concentration risk as all the assets are invested with the insurance company and a default will wipe out all the assets.
Although probability of this is very low as insurance companies have to follow stringent regulatory guidelines which mitigate risk.
During the year, there were no plan amendments, curtailments and settlements.

The Company’s Board of Directors has overall responsibility for the establishment and oversight of the Company’s risk management framework.

(A) Credit risk
i) Actual or expected significant adverse changes in business,
ii) Actual or expected significant changes in the operating results of the counterparty,
iii) Financial or economic conditions that are expected to cause a significant change to the counterparty’s ability to meet its obligations,
iv) Significant changes in the value of the collateral supporting the obligation or in the quality of the third-party guarantees or credit enhancements.
Credit risk is managed at Company level.
The Company’s risk management policies are established to identify and analyse the risks faced by the Company, to set appropriate risk limits and controls and to monitor risks. Risk management policies and systems are reviewed regularly to reflect changes in market conditions and
the Company’s activities. The Board has taken all necessary actions to mitigate the risks identified basis the information and situation present.
